Roadmap

Roadmap

Generics

Generic functions, type arguments and how they are worked out, how a generic function is checked, and the type syntax Name<A, B>, T[?] and T[N].

A generic function is written once and works for many types. The compiler makes one real function for each set of types it is called with, so a generic call is exactly as fast as one written out by hand. This page states the rules for what builds today, then interfaces and constraints, and generic units at the end. The lesson and the guide introduce the ideas.

Generic functions

Type parameters go in <> after the function's name, and can be used anywhere in the signature and the body where a type goes. A function can have several, separated by commas.

A name for a type parameter is a name like any other, so it cannot be a struct, enum or built-in type name, and a list cannot name one twice (E0605). A unit's name is allowed with a warning (W0618): inside the function or struct, the name stands for the type, and X as unit still names the unit (see units). A function with type parameters is not a function until it is called, so its name alone is not a value (E0604), and it is defined once like any other function (E0202).

Working out the type parameters

Each parameter is worked out from the arguments, left to right. The first argument that has a type decides, and a later argument for the same parameter must have exactly that type. T in a parameter written &T or &mut T is what the borrow points at, and in T? it is the type inside the optional.

A number written as a constant, such as 300 or 2.5, has no type of its own. It takes the type the first typed argument fixed, and fails the way uint8 x = 300; does when it does not fit. When every argument that shows T is a constant, T is the type a constant has by itself: uint32 for a whole number and float64 for a decimal.

When the arguments cannot tell, write the types out after the name: max<uint8>(5, 200). A call writes all of the type arguments or none of them. Two arguments that disagree are E0603, and a call where nothing shows a parameter is E0601:

More type arguments than parameters is E0602. Writing only some of them is not supported yet (E0901), and a type argument cannot be a borrow yet (E0901): write &T in the parameter instead.

How a generic function is checked

A generic function with no constraint on its parameters is not checked where it is written (see Constraints for the ones that have one). Each call makes an instance, a function for those types, and the instance is checked as if the types had been written in the function by hand. Two calls with the same types share one instance. Calls with different types make different functions, named max<uint32> and max<float64> in messages and dumps.

This means a body can use any operator or method that every type it is called with has, and an error inside the body appears when a call asks for a type the body does not work for. The error is shown at its own line in the function, with the call that made the instance:

A function nothing calls is never checked, and says so with warning W0600.

A generic function may call itself and other generic functions. A call with the same types reuses the instance, so ordinary recursion works. A call that asks for a bigger type each time (grow<T> calling grow<T?>) would never stop, and is E0608 after 64 instances.

Type syntax

A type name can be followed by type arguments in <>: Map<string, uint32>, Stack<Stack<uint32>>. After a number type, < still opens a unit (float64<m/s>), so Vec<float64<m>> is a Vec of metres. A type that takes no arguments, such as Point, is E0602 when it is given some. A unit can be an argument too, written with unit in front: Track<float64, unit m/s> (see Generic over units).

[?] after a type is a list that grows (string[?]), and [4] is an array of four (uint8[4]); they can be stacked (uint32[?][?]) and followed by ? (string[?]?). A length of 0 is an error. Lists and arrays are described in Arrays and lists; a generic function can take &T[?] and have T worked out from the list. An array length can be a generic value parameter (struct Buffer<T, uint32 N>); see Value parameters.

Generic structs and enums

struct Cell<T> { ... } and enum Maybe<T> { ... } take type parameters the same way, and Cell<uint32> names an instance. Each instance is its own type with its own fields, methods, operators, constructors, drop(), fill and defs, laid out and checked as if you had written Cell_uint32 by hand. Cell<uint32> written in two places is one type; Cell<uint32> and Cell<sint32> are different types. A generic struct's own methods use only the struct's parameters: a method with type parameters of its own is E0901.

Generic struct arguments are never worked out for you: a declaration, new and a static call write the whole type (new Cell<uint32> of (5), Cell<string>::make("held"), Maybe<uint32>::Nothing()). Where the type is known, a bare variant name works as for any enum (Maybe<uint32> m = Just(5);). A generic function can take one, though, and works its parameters out from it: T unwrap<T>(Cell<T> c) called with a Cell<uint32> has T = uint32.

An instance may be an argument of another (Pair<Cell<uint32>, string>). Whether an instance is Copy follows the usual rule applied to that instance: Cell<uint32> is Copy and Cell<string> is not. A def is for one instance (def Origin of Vec2<sint32> { ... }), and struct Cell<T> defaults Start looks for a def of that name for each instance.

As with generic functions, the instance is what gets checked. An error inside a method shows at its own line with the instance that made it:

Writing a generic type without arguments (Cell c;) is E0604, the wrong number of arguments or arguments on a type that takes none is E0602, a struct that holds itself through an instance is E0210 as for any struct, and a type that asks for ever bigger instances of itself is E0608.

Borrows as type arguments

A type argument of a generic struct or enum may be a borrow, or a type that holds one. Stack<&string> is a stack of borrows of strings that live elsewhere, and the stack becomes a borrower: its lifetime is worked out from what is put into it, with nothing written. s::push(&name) ties s to name, so name has to outlive every later use of s.

The methods of the instance are checked as if T were written out as &string. Everything the template declares as T is one lifetime, so push(T x) may keep x inside self, and T? pop() hands the same borrow back. Ending the borrowed string's block before the stack's last use is the usual E0306:

A generic struct made this way may not be used as the field of another struct that is not generic (E0901 for now), and a generic function called with a borrow type argument (same<&string>(&s)) is still E0901: write &T in the parameter. A list of borrows is spelled List<&string>.

Optional types

Optional<uint32> is another way to write uint32?; the two are the same type, and can be mixed freely.

An optional that holds a borrow is written maybe &T: maybe &string is the optional of &string (the same type as Optional<&string>). It is what a list or a stack gives back when the item is a borrow, and messages print it that way. Write maybe &T only with a &: maybe string is an error, since an owned optional is string?.

Interfaces

An interface lists what a type must have: method signatures, static signatures and required fields. It has no method bodies. A struct says which interfaces it implements with with, several joined by and, and the compiler checks it once every declaration has been read.

A struct implements an interface method with a method of the same name, public, with the same parameters and result and the same staticness. Operator methods can be listed too (bool <(Self o);). A struct's own == and != need no method: every struct has them.

  • A method missing, or only written under private:, is E0610.
  • A method with other parameters, another result or a different static is E0611.
  • A required field missing, of another type, or not public is E0614.
  • An unknown name after with or extends is E0201, and an interface name can not be used as the name of a struct, enum or other interface (E0202).

extends makes an interface include another's members: interface Placed extends Shape and Positioned. A struct that implements Placed implements Shape and Positioned too. Two parents with a member of the same name need equal signatures, and an interface that extends itself, directly or through others, is E0615.

Generic interfaces

An interface can take type parameters: interface Read<T>. A type implements one particular instance, with Read<uint32>, and a generic struct can pass its own parameter on, struct Cell<T> with Read<T>. extends works the same way: interface ReadChild<T> extends Read<T>. A bound names the instance it asks for: R with Read<T>.

Read<uint32> and Read<string> are different interfaces. A type that implements one does not implement the other (E0607), a member with the wrong signature for the instance is E0611, and the wrong number of type arguments is E0602 (E0604 when none are written). A generic with a bound such as R with Read<T> is checked where it is written like any other: a method the instance does not list is E0606.

Not supported yet (E0901): borrowing a generic interface (&Read<uint32>), and interface methods with type parameters of their own.

Iterable

Iterable<T> is built in: interface Iterable<T> { T? at(uint64 i); }. A type that implements it can be the thing after of in a for: for (T x of thing) evaluates thing once and calls thing::at(0), at(1), ... until one gives none, binding each payload to x. The value is not used up, and at takes self shared, so the loop body cannot change it (the same rule as for lists). skip, continue, break and break 2 work as in any loop.

T x takes the item (a copy for numbers, the moved value for items that own memory); &T x looks at it. &mut T x is not available (E0901): at hands out values, so changes would be lost. A variable of any other type is E0630.

A type may be Iterable over several item types; the variable's type picks the at. Two methods called at with the same parameters and different results are allowed for this; calling one by name (g::at(0)) is E0632, and a variable that matches none of the item types is E0631.

Self

Inside an interface, Self stands for the type that implements it, so static Self zero(); means static Circle zero() for Circle and static Cube zero() for Cube. It is a reserved word with no meaning outside an interface (E0616): in a struct, write its name.

Methods that change self

A struct method's mode is worked out from its body: it either reads self or changes it. An interface cannot see a body, so a method that may change self says so after its parameters. A struct method may change self only where the interface method says changes self; changing less is fine. A method that writes only mut fields counts as changing. Writing changes self anywhere but in an interface is E0613. (changes is an ordinary name everywhere else.)

Interfaces as types

An interface can only be borrowed, never held: Shape s and Shape[?] are E0617. A borrow of one, &Shape or &mut Shape, accepts a borrow of any struct that implements it, and a call through it runs the method of the real struct while the program runs. Any interface can be borrowed this way.

Where a &Shape is wanted (an argument, a &Shape s = &c; declaration, a return) a &Circle or a &Square is converted by itself. A &mut Counter takes a &mut of a struct and can call the methods that say changes self; through a plain &Counter they are E0311, like any change through a &.

A required field is read through the borrow (p.x), and a &Placed becomes a &Shape or a &Positioned where one of those is wanted, because Placed extends them. The borrow of the struct lasts as long as the &Shape is used, exactly as for a &Circle.

What a &Shape cannot do:

  • A static method, a method that has Self in its signature, or an operator method is not callable through it: the struct behind it is not known (E0619). Call it on the struct, or in a generic constrained with the interface.
  • A struct that does not implement the interface does not convert (E0640).
  • A method that returns a borrow, a required field written to, and a &Circle where Circle itself holds borrows are E0901 for now. A list of &Shape works (List<&Shape>), but == and contains on it are E0901.

A generic function constrained by an interface (T with Shape) is the other way to write code over several kinds: the kind is fixed for each call, and the call is not looked up while the program runs.

Constraints

T with Shape after a type parameter asks for a type that implements the interface; T with Shape and Drawable asks for several. It works on generic functions and on generic structs, and T can be given a constraint while another parameter in the same list has none.

A constrained generic is checked twice, in two different ways.

Where it is written, once, whether or not anything uses it. The body is checked with T standing for a type that has only what the constraints promise: the methods of the interfaces and of the interfaces they extend, their required fields, and their static methods, called as T::zero(). Anything else is E0606, even if every type used so far happens to allow it. An operator on a T is E0606 unless an interface declares that operator method. A T can be passed to another constrained generic only if its own constraints include the other's; a method that says changes self needs a &mut T or a mut binding (E0311, E0312), whatever the type that is used later does. A constrained template nothing uses is therefore not reported as unused (no W0600).

At each use, the type given for T must implement the interfaces (E0607). The instance is then an ordinary function or struct, so a call of s::area() is a direct call, with nothing looked up while the program runs.

A parameter with no constraint is checked per use, as before: what the body does with it is checked when a call gives it a type, and the error points at the body and the call. In a list that mixes the two, what depends on the unconstrained parameter waits for a use, and the rest is checked at the definition.

Types you do not ownTentative: may change

Any type can promise an interface from outside its own declaration, by writing its name, with, the interface and the methods: uint8 with Describe { string describe() { ... } }. The declaration can be anywhere in the project. For a number type, bool or string the methods get the value as self; for a struct they join the struct's own methods. Operators and constructors cannot be given to a built-in type yet, and enums and generic instances cannot promise interfaces this way yet (E0901).

The standard interfaces below are already built in for numbers and string, so T with Ordered works with uint32 and float64 without a declaration. A program that declares its own struct, enum or interface with one of these names uses its own instead; uint32 with Zero { ... } then promises that one.

InterfaceMembersImplemented by
Zerostatic Self zero();numbers, string ("")
Equalbool ==(Self o);numbers, bool, string
Ordered (extends Equal)bool <(Self o); and <=, >, >=numbers
Textstring text();numbers, bool

The set and members above are the first attempt and may change. A struct can implement Equal without writing ==, because every struct has one.

A block like this sees only the struct's public members. Writing Secret with trusted Show { ... } lets its methods use the private fields, methods and constructors too, as the struct's own methods do. trusted is not a reserved word: it counts as the modifier only when an interface name follows it. Using a private member in a plain block is E0212, and the help points at trusted.

Value parameters

A generic can take a whole number as a parameter. It is written like a variable: the integer type, then the name. The classic use is an array length, struct Buffer<T, uint32 N> { T[N] items; }, but the type can be any integer type (uintN or sintN) and the number need not be a length: struct Mod<uint64 P> is arithmetic modulo P.

Where the type is used, the argument is any constant: a number, a calculation on numbers (Buffer<sint32, 2 * 8>), a named constant, or a value parameter of the generic you are inside (Wrap<M> can hold a Buffer<sint32, M>). The values are part of the type, so Buffer<sint32, 4> and Buffer<sint32, 8> are different types, as Cell<uint32> and Cell<sint32> are. In the body, N is a constant of its declared type (return N; in a uint32 method); in the fields and signatures it can also be an array length, T[N]. It is not a type: using it as one is E0609.

A generic function can take them too, and works them out from the arguments: sum<uint32 N>(&sint32[N] a) called with a four-item array has N = 4. Two arguments that show the same N must agree (E0603). When no argument shows it, the call writes it, explicit<21>() (E0601 otherwise).

The errors are short: a value that is not a constant, such as a variable, is E0634; one that does not fit the parameter's type (300 for a uint8, -1 for a uint32) is E0635; a length of 0 for T[N] is E0636; a type where a value goes, or a number where a type goes, is E0602.

Named constants and calculations

A top-level value that is not mut and whose initializer is known when the program is compiled is a named constant. It works as a value everywhere and also in types: as an array length, or as a value argument.

The initializer can use numbers, other constants and arithmetic, in any order in the file. A function call or input (io::inln()) is only known while the program runs, so it cannot be used in a type; a top-level value like that is not supported yet (E0901), and using its name in a type is E0634. A local variable with the same name hides the constant. Two constants with one name are E0638.

Writing fixed in front is optional and makes the compiler check that the value is a constant: fixed uint32 MAX = SIZE * 2; is fine, fixed uint32 N = io::inln()->to<uint32>(); is E0637.

Inside a type, any calculation on value parameters is allowed: T[N + 1] or Buffer<T, N * 2>. It is worked out for each instance, so Padded<sint32, 2> holds a sint32[3] and a Buffer<sint32, 4>. A result that does not fit the parameter (Mod<N * 200> with a uint8 parameter and N = 2) is E0635, and a zero length (T[N - 1] with N = 1) is E0636; both point at the instantiation.

A generic function works a value parameter out only from a plain T[N], or from a simple shape with one name and a number: [N + 1], [N - 1], [10 - N], [N * 2]. Any other calculation ([N / 2]) cannot be worked out, and the call writes the argument, halved<4>(&q) (E0601). A constraint on a value parameter (uint32 N with ...) and a value parameter on an interface are still E0901.

Generic over units

A function can take a unit parameter: unit U after its name stands for a unit, and float64<U> uses it the way a type parameter is used. The function works with any unit and keeps the one it was given.

The unit of a call is worked out from the arguments, just as a type parameter is: the first argument that has a unit decides it, and every other argument that shows U must have the same one (E0603). A plain number has no unit to give, so when no argument shows U the call needs it written: twice<unit m>(x) (E0601). A result can use the unit inside a bigger one, as speed does above. The body is checked for each unit the function is called with, so x * 2.0 keeps the unit, and x + y needs both to have it. A unit parameter is not a type: U copy = a; is E0609. Units written two ways are one unit: N and kg*m/s^2 (see Units of measure) make one instance.

A struct or an enum takes a unit parameter in the same way, and each use writes its unit with unit in the arguments. Units are never worked out for a struct: a declaration writes them.

A parameter can put U inside a bigger unit, such as float64<U/s> v. The call works U out by dividing the argument's unit by the other units of the parameter: dist(3.0<m/s>, 2.0<s>) has U = m. A power of U takes a root: float64<U*U/s> gives U = m from m*m/s. When the argument's units do not split that way (m/s for U*U/s), the call is E0603. A parameter with two unit parameters (float64<U*Q>) needs the others from other arguments, or the call is E0601.

A type argument where a unit goes, or a unit where a type goes, is E0602. Not built yet (E0901): a constraint on a unit parameter (unit U with Shape).

Function types and lambdas

A function type lists its parameter types in parentheses, then => and its result type. A local or parameter of function type is called with ordinary parentheses. A named function can be passed by name wherever its function type is expected.

The parameter and result types must match (E0650 and E0651). Function values can be held in locals and passed down as arguments. Returning one or storing one inside another value is E0652.

Lambda expressions

Write the parameter types and names, followed by =>. An expression body takes its result type from the expression. A block body takes its result type from its return statements, which must agree. A block with no return statements gives none.

Captures

A lambda borrows the enclosing locals it uses. Reads give it a shared borrow. If its body changes a capture, the compiler infers a mutable borrow. The borrow lasts until the last use of the function value.

Changing a borrowed capture before the last call gives E0302. For example, changing extra between creating add and calling it would produce error[E0302]: cannot change `extra` while it is borrowed if extra were declared mut.

A move lambda takes ownership of its captures. Using an owning value again after it has been moved into a lambda gives E0301.

Other capture and result formsNot implemented yet

Borrowing an existing borrow or holder into a closure, capturing a function value, and returning a borrow from a lambda are pending.

Changing fixed move capturesTentative: may change

The mutability rule for fixed bindings captured by move is open. Changing one currently gives E0901.

Collection callbacks

Lists and arrays call an each callback once per item, in order. For a collection of T, the callback takes T or &T and gives none. A by-value parameter gets its own copy of an owning item, while &T reads the original item.

Mutable item callbacksTentative: may change

The callback and borrow rules for mutable item access through each are open. An &mut T callback gives E0901. Use a for loop with &mut T to change items.

Arrays and lists

Array and list types, literals, indexing with bounds checks, changing a list, its methods, comparing, for loops, splitting strings into lists, and maps with their keys, updates and walks. Parts still to come are marked.

Moves and copies

When a value moves, how to keep it with copy, taking a field out, and the errors the compiler reports.
